issue: demo-shop checkout returns HTTP 503 cache_unavailable: Redis OOM command not allowed when used memory > 'maxmemory'

analysis.summary: The demo-shop checkout service returns HTTP 503 errors due to Redis running out of memory and rejecting commands when memory usage exceeds the configured maxmemory limit.

hypotheses.cause: Redis instance used for caching ran out of memory due to excessive data or missing eviction of expired keys, causing command rejections and service unavailability.
hypotheses.reasoning: Similar past incidents show Redis OOM errors caused by memory exhaustion from missing eviction or excessive data, leading to service degradation or outages.

hypotheses.cause: A recent deployment introduced a high-memory-consuming operation or bug that caused Redis memory usage to spike beyond maxmemory limits.
hypotheses.reasoning: Past incidents indicate that deployments causing increased Redis load or traffic can lead to memory pressure and failures.

hypotheses.cause: Redis instance configuration for maxmemory or eviction policy is misconfigured or insufficient for current workload, causing OOM errors under normal load.
hypotheses.reasoning: Misconfiguration or insufficient resource allocation can cause Redis to reject commands when memory limits are reached.

first_checks: Check Redis memory usage and maxmemory configuration to confirm current memory pressure and limits.
Review Redis eviction policy and key expiration metrics to verify if keys are being evicted properly.
Inspect recent deployment logs and code changes for any modifications affecting Redis usage or caching behavior.
Check Redis logs for OOM errors and command rejections to correlate with incident timestamps.
Verify if Redis automatic restart or failover mechanisms are enabled and functioning.
fix_steps: Increase Redis maxmemory limit or scale Redis instance vertically to handle current workload.
Fix or rollback any recent deployment changes that increased Redis memory usage excessively.
Implement or tune Redis eviction policies to ensure expired or unnecessary keys are removed timely.
Enable monitoring and alerting on Redis memory usage and OOM events to detect issues early.
Configure automatic Redis restarts or failover to recover from OOM conditions without manual intervention.

similar_incidents.issue: Server outtage. 🙅‍♀️ Fault Once the mentioned code was deployed to our application servers, it slowly increased the used memory of the Redis instance over a period of three weeks.
similar_incidents.root_cause: We immediately started investigating the issue and found that our main Redis instance, which handles asynchronous job processing and caching, had run out of available memory, and therefore all calls to Redis were failing.
similar_incidents.solution: The review of the code, we failed to notice a missing flag in our Redis queueing code, which removed completed jobs from Redis. After ~20 minutes AWS was able to provision the resized instance, which restored our API availability.

issue: Checkout requests are slow and time out; database connection pool exhausted, timeout waiting for a connection from the pool

analysis.summary: Checkout requests are slow and timing out due to exhaustion of the database connection pool.

hypotheses.cause: Database connection pool exhaustion caused by high traffic and inefficient query patterns leading to saturation of available connections.
hypotheses.reasoning: Similar incidents at GitHub and Stripe involved connection pool saturation due to high traffic and inefficient queries causing request timeouts and slowdowns.

hypotheses.cause: A recent deployment introduced a bug causing database connections not to be returned to the pool, leading to connection starvation and timeouts.
hypotheses.reasoning: A past critical incident involved a deployment mistake causing connection pool starvation and API downtime, which could explain the current symptoms if a recent deploy occurred.

hypotheses.cause: Increased client retries amplifying load on the database connection pool, worsening saturation and causing timeouts.
hypotheses.reasoning: Stripe incident showed client retries can amplify load on an already saturated connection pool, contributing to timeouts.

first_checks: Check current database connection pool usage and saturation metrics.
Review recent deployment logs for changes affecting database connection handling.
Analyze query patterns and slow query logs to identify inefficient queries causing connection retention.
Monitor client retry rates to detect amplification loops.
Check application logs for errors related to database connection acquisition timeouts.
fix_steps: If a recent deployment caused the issue, roll back to the last known good version.
Optimize database queries and indexes to reduce connection hold times.
Increase database connection pool size temporarily to relieve pressure.
Implement rate limiting or circuit breakers on client retries to prevent amplification.
Monitor connection pool metrics continuously and alert on saturation thresholds.

similar_incidents.issue: GitHub services went offline multiple times due to database connection pool saturation.
similar_incidents.root_cause: High traffic combined with an inefficient query pattern on the shared mysql1 database cluster exhausted ProxySQL connection limits.
similar_incidents.solution: Optimized database index queries and added proactive connection rate-limiting for backend API requests.

similar_incidents.issue: Payment API median response time jumps from ~120ms to multiple seconds, checkouts stalling for many customers at once.
similar_incidents.root_cause: A metadata write path used during payment creation saturated a database cluster after a traffic increase combined with a reduced number of available connections in the connection pool. As requests queued, client-side retries added further load to the same overloaded pool, amplifying the slowdown across thousands of integrated platforms.
similar_incidents.solution: Reporting suggests recovery involved relieving the connection pool bottleneck and separating client retry traffic from core request queues to prevent the same amplification loop in future incidents.

hypotheses.cause: Typo in service configuration file causing the application to fail reading critical settings after deployment
hypotheses.reasoning: Similar incidents involved configuration deployment errors causing checkout failures or application startup issues immediately after deploys.

hypotheses.cause: Incomplete propagation of configuration changes leading to inconsistent application behavior
hypotheses.reasoning: Past incident showed partial propagation of config changes caused failures in starting web dynos, which could manifest as errors after deploy.

hypotheses.cause: Regression in application code triggered by new configuration values causing checkout failures
hypotheses.reasoning: A past critical incident involved a regression causing checkout degradation after a patch, though current report points more to config typo.

Check application logs for errors related to configuration loading or missing settings
Confirm that the deployment process completed successfully and the new configuration was applied

similar_incidents.issue: Git push heroku main' silently fails to deploy new code even though the push itself succeeds.
similar_incidents.root_cause: An incorrect deployment process meant that newly introduced configuration variables were not actually being used by the running application, so code that depended on those variables behaved as if they were never set, even though the push and build steps reported success.
similar_incidents.solution: Corrected the deployment process so new configuration variables are properly picked up and used at runtime, and added a way to verify that a deploy is actually using the intended configuration rather than just checking build/push success.

similar_incidents.issue: Web dynos fail to start after a routine remote configuration change, application deploys stuck.
similar_incidents.root_cause: An automated remote configuration change did not fully propagate to all the systems responsible for starting web dynos, leaving some of them working from stale configuration and unable to start new dynos correctly.
similar_incidents.solution: Manually verified and re-propagated the configuration to all affected systems, and added a completion check to confirm remote configuration changes have actually reached every target system before considering the change complete.
